content:
I was wondering if anyone had any thoughts on if we should include experimental data into Physlib, and if so what is the best way of doing it?

I personally think it would be nice, as experimental data is an important part of physics knowledge. Maybe a type ExperiementalData which includes optionally all of the relevant information one could want to add (e.g. measurement, link to dataset, link to paper, corresponding type etc.). We can directly connect this to definitions or theorems now, although I think this is something which could also wait for the future.

There was some previous talk about integrating results from the particle data group, and this might be a good first candidate.
A good source for data which may eventually be of use to Physlib is: https://physics.nist.gov/cuu/pdf/wall_2022.pdf

I think there could be another path that physlib could encompass along with the above, in the field of engineering, there are loads of emprically driven correlations and tables that are in use constantly. To give a some examples we have steam tables, estimating pressure loss in pipes and many more phenomenological results. Most of these are calculated using references now; I think a very interesting path is combining the data in the chart provided above by nist, the actual API present in physlib, and formalize the formulation of these empirical charts (apologies for being vague I have not fully fleshed this out)
Actually when looking through the PDG would largely accomplish the same goal as the above..
Yeah I agree with this overall vision: we should be connecting theory and experiment. I think having a foundation for experimental data in the first place is a least a push in this direction.

I can have a go at this over the weekend (as need some time to think about a design) and open up a PR to PhyslibAlpha as a start, as a test of the design what I can do is try and see if we can have something simple like 9.81 m/s^2 = g and also parts of PDG as well. Though if someone finds this interested feel free to scoop it up from me :)

Edit: clarification on g, i mean connecting the units API to g
It would be great if lean could be used to justify the statistical manipulations used to determine various constants and error terms from experimental data.

I think this is highly related :). Many thanks for sharing this - we should work out at least what we can learn from there

Long term: Thinking about the taxonomy of results in physics, I think there are: definitions, lemmas, experimental data, algorithms, scripts, computional results and remarks. Likely missing some(?). I think it would be generally nice to eventually include all of these some way in Physlib. Not necessarily explicitly, and I think a lot of thought should go into exactly how, but connections with all of these things and the formal definitions and lemmas we have are important.
I think it might be nice to split experiments into two types “Task” (ie the task which was trying to be done) and an “Outcome” given a task, which records the specific outcomes of a given task.
One could also have an instance called ‘HasPrecise Outcome’ for those tasks where the outcome is precisely known (no errors etc)

This is what I currently have in mind for this direction: 

/- Basic structures -/

structure WithError (N : Type) where
  val : N
  oneSigmaError : N

structure PhysicsTask where
  task : String
  outcomeType : Type
  measurmentUnit : Option Units

structure PhysicsTask.Outcome (S : PhysicsTask) where
  outcome : S.outcomeType
  ref : String

class HasUniqueOutcome (S : PhysicsTask) where
  default : S.Outcome

/- Example tasks -/

-- something which is not exact
def massOfElectron : PhysicsTask where
  task := "Measure the pole mass of the electron."
  outcomeType := WithError Real
  measurmentUnit := Real

-- Something which is exact.
def anomalyFreeAtlas : PhysicsTask where
  task := "Find all anomaly free U(1) chanrges which can be associated with the standard
    model particles, which are anomaly free, up to a maximum charge of 10"
  outcomeType : List Charges
  measurmentUnit := None
